The tone is the asset. She is identifiable inside four bars, which almost nobody in this lane manages, and she has taken her time rather than shipped to a schedule. The debut album is coming through Moonshyne and Big Effect. It is the one on this board still to be heard.

entries.name: BLUEBOY — Finn Askew
entries.benchmark: Nothing on the 50 shares this root. Jim Legxacy is the nearest by geography and it is not close
entries.read: BLUEBOY is six songs in seventeen minutes and it knows what it is: pastel, close-miked, woozy, nearer to Mk.gee and Dijon than to anything on daytime radio. Askew is from Wellington in Somerset and played the Jazz Cafe in Camden on July 31. The distance from the 50 is worth stating plainly: this is bedroom alt-pop with an R&B finish, made a long way from the root the canon runs on. What the room has is a cosign stack, SZA, Kehlani, Bieber, attached to a run of singles and one seventeen-minute tape. He told Wonderland he wants a darker second tape before the year is out. That is the record that settles it.

issues.forecast: On East 91st Street, a handmade listening room has thirteen days left; in Durham, a 244-page theory of diaspora inheritance goes to press; on a Miami promo feed, a rapper's younger brother titled his first visuals ANCESTORS. The claim of the week is lineage over launch: where the sound comes from is the argument now, not where it charts.
come_up: Listening rooms as institutions: handmade hi-fi moving from lofts and record bars onto museum floors
Sibling economies in rap: brothers shooting, writing, and promoting each other's rollouts
Open-access university press editions, free to read on publication day
decline: Streaming as posture: the playback object that asks for your attention is back on the main floor
Drill as Chicago's only export; the city's youngest star is cutting Miami bass records
Blind algorithmic discovery; promo pages and family chains are doing the finding again
issues.climate: Lineage over launch: a museum-grade listening room in its final days, a Duke theory of diaspora inheritance, and a rap week run on bloodlines.

entries.name: Art of Noise — Cooper Hewitt
entries.benchmark: Material Culture — craft objects with a listening lineage, shown instead of sold
entries.read: Thirteen days left. Art of Noise closes August 16 at Cooper Hewitt after turning the Smithsonian's design museum at 2 East 91st Street into the best listening session in New York: more than 300 works across the entire third floor, a century of objects that taught people how to hear, from the Castiglioni brothers' RR-126 radio-phonograph to the first Walkman and the first iPod, plus Milton Glaser's Dylan poster and Peter Saville's Unknown Pleasures sleeve. The center of gravity sits downstairs, where Brooklyn engineer Devon Turnbull, who builds under the name OJAS, hand-built HiFi Pursuit Listening Room Dream No. 3: a monolithic audio system programmed daily with live operators, a shrine to sitting still. teenage engineering designed the exhibition environment and a custom playback device loaded with New York songs. Museums keep discovering what record shops always knew, and this one wrote it in hardware. The claim underneath the whole show: design is not how music looks. It is how attention gets built.

entries.name: ffawty
entries.benchmark: Jim Legxacy — the same diaspora-fusion move, St. Thomas-to-Miami instead of Lagos-to-London
entries.read: Three places built the voice: St. Thomas gave it the lilt, Atlanta the melody, Miami the pressure. ffawty writes pain music that can still run a function, and the resume behind the 120,000 monthly listeners is heavier than the number: pen credits on Billboard-charting records for Sexyy Red and Sukihana, a Lyrical Lemonade freestyle, and a 2026 single run from Rock-a-bye to July's HAKUNA MATATA that treats every three weeks like a deadline. Pray For ffawty, the 18-track album from last September, is the body of work the room has not opened yet. The gap is that the co-signs arrived before the audience did.

entries.name: Afroindigenization — Catherine A. John
entries.benchmark: Black Film Archive — scholarship as taste infrastructure, print instead of screen
entries.read: A theory book that treats a krump circle as evidence. Catherine A. John, professor of Africana Studies at the University of Rhode Island, spent decades building the case that indigenous African knowledge survived the Middle Passage as embodied practice, then found it in mermaid lore in Woodside, Jamaica, in the trance states of Los Angeles krump captured in the film Rize, and in the 2014 tournament run of two Black college debaters. Duke is also releasing an open-access edition, free to read on day one, which suits a book about knowledge held in common. Publishes August 25 by Duke University Press — 244 pages, $31.95.

entries.name: Ghetto Love Story — BabyChiefDoit
entries.benchmark: Chris Crack — Chicago auteurs who refuse to stay in one lane
entries.read: A Chicago teenager who produces most of his own beats dropped a Miami bass record into the middle of a drill album, and it stuck: 11 million Spotify streams in seven weeks, three verses of neighborhood soap opera that keep piling on plot twists. Rise Against My Broken Odds, out June 12 on APG, is album three. The room heard this one correctly.

entries.name: ANCESTORS — P!MP
entries.benchmark: Jiah — earliest-stage underground rap, and the distance is a catalog
entries.read: The ANCESTORS visuals move right: one performer, one brick wall, a camera by @publicgoat that trusts the face to carry the frame, and the full video is up on YouTube. P!MP is ffawty's blood brother, and the freestyles stacking up on his Instagram are the better evidence right now — loose, quick, and sharper than the release schedule suggests. What exists so far is one strong video and a feed; the streaming footprint is still forming. Come back when there is a body of work to score.

issues.forecast: The strongest argument on the board this week is not written down. It is worn. A Lagos photographer gave up color to look at one white robe; an Accra jeweler rebuilt Akan trade beads into something meant to be inherited; a Cleveland reporter went home to find out what a badge does to a family across four generations. Insignia over image: the object that declares where a person came from is doing the arguing, and the work that cannot name its source is losing the room.
come_up: Dress as primary document: photographers and jewelers treating what people wear as the evidence rather than the styling
Provenance as a product feature: licensed, traceable training data sold as the reason to use the tool
Northern Nigeria as a sound source rather than a subject, with the kalangu and the goje carrying the hook
decline: Unsourced models, and the phrase 'we respect artists' with no paperwork behind it
The co-sign stack standing in for a catalog
The logo swap as a cultural event; a Jumpman on a national crest is a licensing deal, not a design idea
issues.climate: Insignia over image: a white robe, a trade bead, a badge and a traceable training set, all arguing from provenance.

entries.name: Stephen Tayo — What Comes to Mind When You See the Garments?
entries.benchmark: Players Magazine — the 50's editorial-taste lane, where what people wear is treated as the primary document
entries.read: Tayo shot the entire series in black and white, and the subtraction is the argument: color has been his signature since he started photographing Lagos street style, and giving it up leaves nothing in the frame but one garment. The sutana, also called aso-funfun, is the flowing white robe worn by followers of the Aladura movement, a Yoruba Pentecostal faith built on divine healing and Yoruba creation stories. He shot devotees across Lagos, Ibadan, Ekiti and into Benin Republic. The show opened August 1 at Alára and runs to September 20; it is his first solo presentation with FF Projects and the fourth in Faridah Folawiyo's year-long residency there. He studied philosophy at Unilag, and it shows in a title that is a question rather than a caption. The V&A, Palais de Tokyo and the Brooklyn Museum all arrived early on him, and the pictures have not softened for any of them.

entries.name: The Black Shield — Wilbert L. Cooper
entries.benchmark: Noname Book Club — the 50's reading lane, and the same appetite for books that argue about power rather than describe it
entries.read: On his mother's side there has been a Cleveland cop in the family since 1950. Both of Wilbert L. Cooper's parents retired from the force, and his sister wore the uniform too. In 2020 he went home to profile the president of the Black Shield, a Black police association that had broken ranks with the rest of the department and lined up behind the reform demands coming out of the protests. Two complications arrived together: the man he came to profile had shot an unarmed young Black man years earlier, and the members received Cooper not as a reporter but as Sergeant Will Cooper's son. What he builds from there braids two histories. One is a family that came north in the Great Migration and took policing because it was among the few routes to a house and a pension in a segregated city. The other is an organization that has spent decades cycling between rebellion and accommodation. A book this well-sourced on a subject this contested is arriving with almost no noise outside the trade; Kirkus gave it a star and nothing else has moved. Publishes August 25 by Farrar, Straus and Giroux — 416 pages, $32.

entries.name: GEMZ — Kiala Kanzi
entries.benchmark: Material Culture — the 50's heritage-craft lane, objects that carry a lineage before a designer touches them
entries.read: Akan trade beads carry information before a designer touches them. Some can be worn only by priests and priestesses; others announce rank and occupation, which is why people in Ghana say the beads talk. Kiala Kanzi researched them, sat with an artisan named Santiago to learn every step of the recycled-glass process, and built GEMZ from there: handmade glass flowers in red, green, white and black, made to be worn in braids. Born in Germany to German, Cameroonian and Syrian parents, she moved from Berlin to Accra two years ago and says her output rose as the pressure fell. She frames the collection as a question rather than a drop: what seeds are we planting, and where.

entries.name: Aiode
entries.benchmark: Moises AI — the 50's creator-AI lane, tools built for people already making something
entries.read: Every AI music company says it respects musicians. Aiode can produce the paperwork, which is the whole reason BandLab Technologies bought it on July 15 and left it running as a standalone product with both founders in place. All of the audio behind its models is licensed and traceable to source, and the musician models are made with the players directing how their own style gets used. The workflow is deliberately narrow: bring a track you are already writing, then hire a virtual session player to take one pass at one section and keep the rest untouched. The roster is still shallow, which is the honest ceiling on a good idea, and native recording is promised without a date.

entries.name: FirstKlaz
entries.benchmark: Victony — the 50's global-diaspora lane, the same crossing attempted from a different corner of Nigeria
entries.read: Abuja, not Lagos. FirstKlaz builds around the kalangu and the goje, the Hausa talking drum and the two-stringed fiddle, and the Gen-Z Arewa run pushed Northern instrumentation into Afropop without sanding it down. Olamide, Joeboy and ODUMODUBLVCK co-signed, and he toured seven states. Against all of that sits one seven-track EP, Déjàvu. The ability is not the question; the catalog is. An album closes this gap, and there isn't one yet.

issues.forecast: The rollout stopped working this week. Nothing on this board was made fast: a curator spent ten years assembling thirty marbles by a sculptor who died in 1907 and whose masterpieces are still missing; a singer spent five years on twelve songs and put them out on his own label after the deal ended; a bookbinder trained in Japan, then London, then opened a studio in Taiwan to build one ring of folded paper. Duration over drop. The work that took its time is the work the room is finally reading, and the release calendar has nothing useful to say about any of it.
come_up: Artist-owned imprints: catalogs coming back to the maker once the label deal ends
Decade-scale curatorial projects built from auction rescues rather than existing holdings
The endband, the training floor, the room tone: the structural detail promoted to the subject
decline: The four-week rollout as evidence of seriousness
The prize shortlist read as the whole of a practice
The festival premiere treated as a finish line rather than a first screening
issues.climate: Duration over drop: ten years of curating, five years of mixing, a training floor on the Senegalese coast, all landing in the same week.

entries.name: Edmonia Lewis: Said in Stone
entries.benchmark: Lauren Halsey — the 50's sculptor; Lewis is the ancestor that lane never got to cite
entries.read: In 2016 Shawnya L. Harris saw a small bust come up at auction and asked her director whether the Georgia Museum of Art could buy it. Ten years later she is co-curator of the first major retrospective Edmonia Lewis has ever had, opening in Athens on August 8 and running to January 3. Roughly thirty marbles, pulled from public and private collections in the United States and abroad, several of them never exhibited anywhere. Lewis was born in Greenbush, New York in 1844, started working in Boston in 1863, and sailed for Rome in 1866 to take a studio off the Piazza di Spagna, becoming the first sculptor of Black and Mississauga descent to win international recognition. She died in 1907 and the work scattered. Some of it was recovered decades later. Some is still missing. The catalog is from the University of Chicago Press; the show goes on to Raleigh next spring. The gap is that the room has spent a century treating Lewis as a biography, and this is the first time it can treat her as a body of work.

entries.name: I Can See — Nick Hakim
entries.benchmark: Baby Rose
entries.read: The ATO deal ended and a relationship ended, and what came through is twelve songs on Hakim's own Earseed Records, out July 24, distributed by Stem. Five years of work: bedroom demos first, then Sonic Ranch in Tornillo, Texas, then Electric Lady and Sear Sound in New York. Andrew Sarlo co-produced, Heba Kadry mastered. The detail that decides it is what stayed in the mix. An out-of-tune piano. A chair. A car going past outside. Hakim has spent a decade as the producer other people call, and this is the record where his own catalog overtakes the session work. Stereogum made it album of the week.

entries.name: Atcha Atcha — Mamadou Dia
entries.benchmark: Black Film Archive
entries.read: Locarno opened today and the film worth the trip screens Sunday. Atcha Atcha is Mamadou Dia's first documentary, shot at the École des Sables in Senegal, where dancers from across the continent take a final year of training under Germaine Acogny. It premieres August 9 in Fuori Concorso and is eligible for the Pardo for Change. Dia took the Pardo d'Oro in Cineasti del Presente here in 2019 with Baamum Nafi; Demba went to the Berlinale in 2024; he joined the Academy in 2025. Maayo in Dakar and Les Films du Bilboquet in Paris produced it. Wawkumba Film, run by Oumou Diégane Niang, carries it across the continent, as it did the two features before. A body is an archive somebody has to teach.

entries.name: Soft Spots — Leila Renee
entries.benchmark: Noname Book Club
entries.read: Robin Clarke runs from an abusive family to a teaching job in South Bend, Indiana, and the novel is about what she does with the distance. Leila Renee published it Tuesday through HarperCollins. Syracuse MFA, a Fulbright, the Gulf Coast Prize in Fiction, short stories in McSweeney's and the Kenyon Review; Deesha Philyaw blurbed it. Renee began drafting in 2020 while reading Edward P. Jones's The Known World, and names Burger's Daughter for structure, Sula and My Brilliant Friend for the friendship, Luster for a protagonist who keeps walking into her own way. On the nightstand right now: Henry Dumas, the Arkansas writer shot by a New York transit officer in 1968 at thirty-three, whose stories she is reading specifically to keep the name moving. That is the reading list of somebody who intends to write more than one book.

entries.name: Endless — Adelene Koh
entries.benchmark: Tamera
entries.read: An endband is the few millimeters of stitching at the head and tail of a book's spine, usually chosen to disappear. Endless is that stitch let off the leash: folded paper and embroidery thread sewn around a single aluminum wire in English technique from the 18th and 19th centuries, closed into a ring. Koh trained in Japan, then London, and runs dddots out of Taiwan. Thirty finalists, 5,100 entries.

issues.forecast: In Salerno, a bathroom that opens onto a Turkish prison. In Brooklyn, a five-year bid counted out as twenty-three and one. On a fourth floor in Harlem, seventeen artists holding the in-between open. What links them is not subject but method: each takes an enclosure and works inside it rather than around it, and those are the strongest objects on this board. The weakest does the reverse, taking a shoe built for a distance and removing the distance. Structure over surface.
come_up: Confinement written as architecture rather than backstory: the cell as a room you can walk into
The multi-curator show: five names organizing, seventeen artists, no house style imposed
Aso oke and adire cut as construction, not printed as reference
decline: The lifestyle edition that keeps the silhouette and removes the reason for it
Coming home framed as a comeback rather than an unresolved argument
The prize longlist read as the whole reception of a book
issues.climate: Structure over surface: a cell installed in a bathroom, a bid reduced to twenty-three and one, an in-between made into somewhere to stand.

entries.name: Fade — Studio Museum in Harlem
entries.benchmark: Project a Black Planet — the 50's curatorial entry; Fade runs the same instinct at emerging-artist scale
entries.read: 144 West 125th Street, fourth-floor gallery, through September 6. Seventeen artists of African and Afro-Latinx descent, born between 1983 and 2000, and most of them working outside New York: New Orleans, Baltimore, Pittsburgh, Chicago. Fade is the sixth of the Studio Museum's “F” shows, a run that opened with Freestyle in 2001 and has been the most reliable early indicator in American art since. Five co-curators assembled it, which is why it carries no single house style. The title does three jobs at once: a cinematic transition, a haircut, a jumper taken going backwards. A month left on it.

entries.name: Sha Hef — Hustlin Ain't a Sin
entries.benchmark: Starlito — the 50's plainspoken street-rap lane; Hef is the New York cousin, funnier and more devout
entries.read: Born in Brooklyn, made his name uptown. Hustlin Ain't a Sin is the first album since Sha Hef finished a five-year sentence, and the religious material is the spine of it rather than a detail: the title track opens on a child's bedtime prayer, then asks whether a dealer who prayed the whole time gets into heaven. He does not answer it. Thirteen tracks, out in June on Black Market Records. Harry Fraud produces three, including “Gotti,” and leaves the vocal clear; Grimm Doza, Nicholas Craven and 183rd take most of the rest. Ab-Soul, Jay Worthy and ANKHLEJOHN guest. “Gotti,” “LIDS” and “No Discussion” are the standouts.

entries.name: The Renovation — Kenan Orhan
entries.benchmark: Noname Book Club — the nearest thing on the 50, and the fit is by reading habit rather than root
entries.read: The most literal book on this year's Booker longlist is also the strangest. Dilara, a Turkish exile in a village outside Salerno, hires builders to add a second bathroom so she can care for her father, who has dementia. They install a Turkish prison cell instead, staffed, and somehow wired to a prison in Istanbul. Kenan Orhan writes from Kansas and has not let the Gezi-to-purges decade go; his 2023 story collection was a PEN/Robert W. Bingham finalist. The device reads as a stunt for roughly ten pages and then stops being one. Longlisted July 28 from 163 submissions; shortlist September 22. Hamish Hamilton, March 26, 256 pages, £16.99.

entries.name: Africa Fashion Week London 2026
entries.benchmark: Derschutze — diasporic fashion with a thesis; AFWL is the trade floor underneath that lane, not a peer to it
entries.read: London supplies the runway; the textile work happens elsewhere. Africa Fashion Week London returns to central London August 17 to 23 for its sixteenth year, founded by Ronke Ademiluyi-Ogunwusi and by now less a show than a trade floor: buyers, retailers, the British Council's Creative DNA program, the Adire Oodua Textile Hub. The names worth the trip are the ones treating heritage cloth as construction rather than print. Klassic Unisex Couture cuts handwoven aso oke and adire into unisex couture. Kente Uncut is a personalised kente developed by Aduhema, a third-year undergraduate. Add an Apron, founded in 2024 by the artist Adéọlá, hand-paints organic cotton and is arguing, in earnest, for the apron as an accessory. Check in December, when the Lagos sister platform runs, and see which of the three has stockists.

entries.name: Karhu Mestari Run LS
entries.benchmark: Karhu — already on the 50 for the running archive; this is the shoe that walks away from it
entries.read: The Mestari Run LS is well made: refined proportions, cleaner paneling, subtler branding, a campaign shot in Japan, on sale since July 17. It is also the performance shoe with the performance taken out. Karhu turns 110 this year, and its better object of the summer was the Fusion 2.0 OG, a straight tribute to the 1996 original. Come back when the archive team gets the next release.

issues.forecast: Accra hands its oldest neighborhood over for a week and charges nothing at the gate. New York spends seven years and two floors to get a room back on the Upper West Side. Room over reach: the strongest work on this board is attached to an address, and the loudest gap is a Camera d'Or with nowhere in America to play it.
issues.climate: Room over reach: a neighborhood given away for a week, ten thousand square feet bought on Columbus Avenue, a website printed on paper, an album built as somewhere to walk.
come_up: The permanent address: independent publishers and collectives taking rooms instead of renting reach
Digital-first publications going to print in their fifth year, with the interview archive as the asset
Records built as places to move through, transitions carrying the structure instead of choruses
decline: The Camera d'Or treated as a distribution plan
The capital campaign announcement read as a program
The street festival covered as a photo opportunity rather than as fifteen years of community production

entries.name: Ben'Imana — Marie-Clémentine Dusabejambo
entries.benchmark: City of God — the 50's film entry; both put a place on screen through the people who came out of it
entries.read: The first word spoken in Ben'Imana is forgiveness, and the woman saying it has her arms locked across her chest. Marie-Clémentine Dusabejambo's debut took the Caméra d'Or at Cannes in May out of Un Certain Regard, and it is the first film by a Rwandan director to enter the festival's official selection. It is set in Kibeho in 2012, the final year of the gacaca courts, the village tribunals convened to try genocidal crimes committed neighbor against neighbor. Vénéranda organizes testimony sessions for the women of the village before they face the court; her sister Suzanne thinks forgiveness cannot be arranged in a room. Clémentine U. Nyirinkindi leads a cast of mostly nonprofessional actors, and the film was made across Rwanda, Gabon, France, Norway and Côte d'Ivoire, in Kinyarwanda throughout. The gap is that the prize for the best first feature at the largest festival in the world has not yet produced an American release, and mk2 was still selling it in May. Watch the fall festival announcements for a distributor.

entries.name: Chale Wote 2026
entries.benchmark: Lauren Halsey — public work built out of one neighborhood and addressed to it first
entries.read: Jamestown and Osu are handed over from Monday, August 10 to Monday, August 17. The fifteenth Chale Wote runs on a schedule most institutions would not print: artists build the work on site between August 1 and 9, then show it for a week in the street. Entry is free and has been since 2011, when ACCRA [dot] ALT started it with Redd Kat Pictures and the Chale Wote Street Art Projekt. The name is Ga for friend, let's go, and it is also what Ghanaians call the rubber flip-flop, which settles who it was addressed to before anyone flew in. James Fort still stands at the water's edge, the harbor still works, and the murals from earlier years are permanent addresses now.

entries.name: Solar Calf — Patrick Belaga
entries.benchmark: Jim Legxacy — the same world-building instinct; the distance is genre, not method
entries.read: Nobody needed another record about video games. Patrick Belaga made one about their maps instead. Solar Calf, out July 31 on PAN, is his second solo album and is built as a place rather than a sequence: nine zones, with transitional passages doing the work a chorus usually does. The reference is the geography of the Zelda series, its dungeons and forest enclaves and mountain villages, not Koji Kondo's themes. Belaga is a classically trained cellist, and the palette is woodwind, brass, piano, strings and percussion played live, then re-sampled and cut against itself in the DAW until the natural flow breaks. “Lake” is marimba and cello at almost Balearic tempo. “Upsurge” takes a calm forest theme apart.

entries.name: Black Is — Lia J. Latty
entries.benchmark: Nataal — a diasporic photography publication that took itself to print
entries.read: Five years online, then paper. Black Is went to print in May with an issue titled Legacy and Continuity in Black Photographic Practice, launched at Charm City Cultural Cultivation in Waverly over Artscape weekend. Lia J. Latty started the site from Baltimore in January 2021 and still runs it alone. The database of every photographer she has interviewed is the real asset.

entries.name: Aperture — 380 Columbus Avenue
entries.benchmark: Monocle — an independent publisher that treats a physical address as part of the editorial
entries.read: Aperture has published photography for seventy-four years and has not had a gallery of its own since it left West 27th Street in 2019. That ends on September 18, when it opens ten thousand square feet across two floors of an 1886 building at 380 Columbus Avenue and 78th Street, designed by LEVENBETTS, with a bookstore, an events space and the production offices in the same rooms. The inaugural hang, curated by Sarah Meister, is called Aperture Loves New York and leans on Arbus, Robert Frank, Dawoud Bey, Carrie Mae Weems and Deana Lawson. All of that is real. None of it is a program yet. The attention this summer is on a capital campaign and a lease, six weeks ahead of anything being on a wall. Come back on September 18 and look at what is hanging.

issues.forecast: The three strongest things on this board were made out of what somebody else was finished with. Salvaged billboard steel in Accra, packing paper off a pleating press in Tokyo, a case of Okinawan cloth whose provenance had been lost for most of a century. Offcut over output, and the loudest name here belongs to a record nobody has heard yet.
issues.climate: Offcut over output: billboard steel rebuilt as a canopy, packing waste soaked in wax and turned into stools, fifty Ryukyu textiles finally matched to the prince who sold them. What is loudest is still two weeks from release.
come_up: Salvage as a structural system rather than a sustainability line in a press release
The annual commission: institutions building a repeating slot instead of a one-off show
Provenance research published as the exhibition itself
decline: The feature-stacked single offered as proof the album is good
Album trailers carrying more story than the records they announce
The marquee guest credit banked instead of built on

entries.name: Limbo Engawa — TAELON7
entries.benchmark: The Shed — the 50's built-culture entry, and the distance is the point: one cost half a billion dollars, the other is cut from roadside advertising
entries.read: The canopies are cut from old billboards. TAELON7, the practice Juergen Benson-Strohmayer runs between Austria and West Africa, stripped steel out of Accra's advertising hoardings, sliced it into strips and wove it onto frames light enough for one person to carry and assemble on site. Underneath sit oversized daybeds copied from the woven beds that construction crews already sleep on inside unfinished buildings across the region. The whole assembly went into the Limbo Museum, a 600-square-meter unfinished neo-brutalist estate in Labone that Dominique Petit-Frère and Emil Grip took over rather than completed. Metalwork by Joseph Awumee, weaving led by Briena Montana, support from the Austrian Cultural Forum in Accra. It ran March 12 to April 12; this fall the same components come apart and go back up at Art Omi in Ghent, New York, as a freestanding pavilion in open fields. Petit-Frère has said plainly what it is for: an annual architectural commission in Africa, on the Serpentine model. That is the part worth watching. One pavilion is a project; a commission that returns every year is an institution, and that is the thing she says the continent has not had.

entries.name: Textiles of Ryukyu Kingdom
entries.benchmark: Material Culture — an object valued for the line you can draw from the hand that made it to the hand that kept it
entries.read: For ninety years the Japan Folk Crafts Museum has known that its finest Okinawan cloth came through Ryoichi Mizutani, and not which pieces were which. Mizutani, a collaborator in the Mingei movement, bought them on Sōetsu Yanagi's recommendation from Goeku Chosho, fifteenth head of a branch house of the Shō clan that ruled the Ryukyu Kingdom until its independence ended in 1879. This show identifies them. Roughly fifty bingata and woven works, hung with other objects tied to the Shō family, opening August 22 and running to November 3 for the museum's ninetieth anniversary. A prince's wardrobe, cataloged at last, in a building that holds seventeen thousand things and explains almost none of them on the wall.

entries.name: The Paper Log: Shell and Core
entries.benchmark: JJJJound — the 50's object-first design entry; the Paper Log arrives at the same place from the factory floor instead of the archive
entries.read: Tokyo, Thursday, Gallery 3 at 21_21 Design Sight in Akasaka, free, through September 13. The object is a compressed roll of pleated paper eighty centimeters tall, produced as packing waste by Issey Miyake's garment pleating. Ensamble Studio peels it into sculpture; Satoshi Kondo's team soaks it in wax and glue and builds stools. Cut one open and the cross-section rings like a tree.

entries.name: nomi. — sweet talk
entries.benchmark: Baby Rose — a voice with an unusual grain, given room by producers who trust it to carry a track alone
entries.read: nomi. sang on Dom Maker's half of MK 3.5, the Mount Kimbie double album Warp put out in November 2022, on a tracklist she shared with slowthai, Danny Brown, James Blake, keiyaA and Liv.e. That credit arrived four years before the catalog did. sweet talk, four songs on earth angel records, landed April 24: a soft, close vocal over drums that hit far harder than the singing suggests, and a guitar figure at the end that comes straight out of Prince. 'what u want' followed on July 10. She played her second show ever last week. The writing is already ahead of the audience.

entries.name: Skilla Baby — The Price of Fame
entries.benchmark: Starlito — the nearest thing on the 50, and the distance is a major-label rollout Starlito built an entire catalog without
entries.read: On May 22, 2025, Skilla Baby was shot three times and crashed his SUV into a building. He recovered. The Price of Fame, out August 21 on Geffen, is built on that, and the cover restages the 1994 photograph of 2Pac leaving a Manhattan courthouse in a wheelchair: a reference earned rather than borrowed. He told XXL this summer the record is for the working man and that he was finished being unrelatable, which is a real pivot from a rapper who came up under Sada Baby making some of the coldest regional records in a city full of them. The reason he sits here rather than higher is that none of it has landed. What is out is the rollout — 50 Cent in the trailer, Chris Brown and Bryson Tiller on 'Face Card,' seven producers on 'Show Me Love' — and his last full-lengths, The Coldest in April and Crack Music 3, are two years back. The room has priced an album it has not heard. Come back on August 21 and score the record instead.

issues.forecast: The strongest signal this week is a lease, not a release: Príncipe holding the keys to its own shop in Lisbon, the V&A spending a whole new museum's opening statement on Black British sound — permanence over promotion, and the room is slow to both.
issues.climate: Room over rollout. The week's leaders signed for space: a batida label with a storefront, a new museum opened on an archive, a convenience chain that became national furniture. The release calendar, meanwhile, is running on autopilot.
come_up: Labels and scenes taking leases: the storefront as the new flagship release
Archival canon-keeping at institutional scale, built on decade-spanning research
Lisbon batida's long arc from housing-project phones to European club institution
decline: The collab calendar on autopilot: box logos on other houses' silhouettes
Dessert-themed sneakers as a release strategy
"Hidden gems" tourism listicles that never leave the tour-bus radius

entries.name: Príncipe Discos
entries.benchmark: City of God — the 50's periphery-to-world diaspora entry; Príncipe is the same journey pressed to vinyl
entries.read: Every Príncipe record leaves the building hand-painted. Márcio Matos stencils each sleeve individually, so no two copies of a batida 12-inch are the same object, a label policy held since 2011 across a catalog that rewired Angolan kuduro, Cape Verdean funaná and semba into the percussion language Lisbon's periphery now exports to the world. The sound was born in Quinta do Mocho, a social housing project outside the postcard city, on cracked copies of FruityLoops; DJ Marfox and DJ Nervoso carried it downtown, and four friends pressed it to vinyl when no Portuguese institution would touch it. Now the institution is theirs. Príncipe opened its own shop and venue space in Lisbon and marked the keys with 'Não Estragou Nada,' a compilation running kuduro, tarraxo and batida under one roof, while label nights still pack Musicbox and Lux Frágil, where Xexa played live this March and Marfox, Nervoso and Dariiofox held the floor after her. Mastering is done by Tó Pinheiro da Silva at his home studio. Skip the tiled miradouros: the rarest culture in Lisbon is the kind the city built itself.

entries.name: The Music Is Black: A British Story
entries.benchmark: Black Film Archive — the 50's canon-keeper; this is the same recovery work at museum scale, for British sound instead of American film
entries.read: V&A East opened its five-storey Stratford museum in April and spent the whole first statement on Black British sound: 125 years, four acts, more than 200 objects, 60 of them newly acquired. Jme's Super Nintendo and Mario Paint cartridge from his first 90s experiments sit near Joan Armatrading's childhood guitar and Samuel Coleridge-Taylor's conducting batons from the early 1900s, while a headset runs 120 tracks cut with full access to the BBC archive. Curator Jacqueline Springer built it as canon-keeping rather than nostalgia: lovers rock, 2 Tone, Brit funk, jungle, trip hop, UK garage and grime treated as one continuous engineering project, staged a short walk from the stadium where Dizzee Rascal played the 2012 opening ceremony. It runs to January 3 at £22.50, £10 under 26, and this summer the Olympic Park around it hosts a festival on the same theme with Sadler's Wells East and the BBC.

entries.name: Ravyn Lenae — Blue Island
entries.benchmark: Baby Rose — the 50's alt-R&B voice; Lenae is the neighbor who just moved to a bigger house on the same block
entries.read: "Never Let Me Go" builds on Chuck Jackson's "Love of You," a 1978 soul record you mostly cannot stream, and ends with Lenae's grandfather on the phone asking whether the albums are selling. They are: "Love Me Not" reached No. 5 on the Hot 100 a full year after release, and Blue Island, out August 7 on Atlantic, answers arrival with a pop swing. 2000s indie guitars on "Handle," Doechii kept restrained on "Babygirl," Dominic Fike playing the loyal dog on "Reputation." Critics split on whether the pivot fully commits; the back half settles it, and Clash landed at 8/10. A 22-date North American run opens at Portola on September 20 with Nourished By Time on select dates.

entries.name: Tony
entries.benchmark: Monocle — nearest thing on the 50 is its editorial-taste lane, and the fit is the subject, not the medium: a cook who became a taste authority
entries.read: A24 opened Tony in six theaters across New York and Los Angeles on August 7, with Dominic Sessa as the young Anthony Bourdain and Matt Johnson, who made BlackBerry, directing. An origin story about a line cook becoming a voice people trusted on where to eat and how to travel, released at the size of a limited menu. Wider rooms follow if these fill.

entries.name: 7-Eleven Thailand — CP All
entries.benchmark: Fortnum & Mason — a nation's pantry as identity; Bangkok got there in 37 years at a fortieth of the price, and it isn't close in tone
entries.read: Patpong Road, 1989: one store. Thailand today: more than 15,000, roughly one per 5,000 people, all run by CP All under a license Dallas granted and Bangkok perfected. The croissant toastie is pressed hot by staff on request, the tamago sando runs 29 baht, and the yadom rack by the register sells Poy-Sian and Hong Thai herbal inhalers against the heat. Bill payment, parcels, insurance renewals: a utility that happens to sell dinner, air-conditioned and open all night. The room found it — 7-Eleven hauls are their own genre now, and Nike cut an Air Max 95 in the livery — but the room is right. What it is not is gatekept; fifteen thousand doors is the opposite of a door policy, and the score holds there.

issues.forecast: Philadelphia, London and a Harlem three years empty are doing more cultural labor this cycle than any release calendar.
issues.climate: Room over rollout, again, but this time the room is memory: a festival's 15th year spent on a single life instead of a premiere, a museum curator naming who gets to define the canon before the show even opens, a harpist writing inside a lineage instead of just citing it. The one clear counter-read is a rap catalog that hasn't caught up to its own tour routing yet.
come_up: Archival authorship: BlackStar's 15th year platforms the maker's whole practice, not the clip
Canon-questioning curation: Charlene Prempeh's Design Museum brief, opening November
Instrument lineage: Brandee Younger carrying Dorothy Ashby's unfinished songbook forward
decline: Comment-count as credibility
The single without a catalog behind it
Tribute framing over just writing inside the lineage

entries.name: Brandee Younger
entries.benchmark: a CROWN next to Material Culture — same instinct, carrying an object's whole history forward instead of just citing it
entries.read: The most radical thing happening in jazz right now is inheritance, not invention. Brandee Younger's Gadabout Season, the New York Times and NPR pick for best jazz album of 2025, plays like something handed down rather than discovered: she performs on Alice Coltrane's actual harp and carries Dorothy Ashby's unfinished songbook the way a family carries a name. Her prior record, Brand New Life, rebuilt lost Ashby compositions with Pete Rock and 9th Wonder in the room; Gadabout Season drops the tribute framing and just writes inside that lineage, gospel and hip-hop sample logic braided into conservatory technique. She's touring Europe this month, Zürich then Bern, carrying an instrument most jazz rooms still treat as a novelty act. The room caught up before the record did: a Grammy nomination, the 2024 NAACP Image Award, a New York Times profile headlined on the Coltrane harp itself. That's not a gap closing. That's a gap that was never open.

entries.name: A Life in Art: Through the Eye of Dr. Leslie King Hammond
entries.benchmark: a CROWN next to Black Film Archive — same curatorial instinct, aimed at a single life instead of a catalog
entries.read: BlackStar turned fifteen this August, Aug 6 to 9 in Philadelphia, 91 films deep, and the one that outlasts the festival week is a portrait, not a premiere. A Life in Art: Through the Eye of Dr. Leslie King Hammond, directed by Ben Baker-Lee and her son Rassaan Hammond, follows the art historian who mentored Amy Sherald through the Michelle Obama portrait commission and has spent five decades teaching artists of color how to defend their own work. The lineage runs both directions here: a son documenting the woman who taught a generation how to look. No streaming date yet. Catch it at a festival first.

entries.name: Charlene Prempeh — The Nue Black Aesthetic
entries.benchmark: a CROWN next to Nataal — same project, arguing for who gets to define the canon rather than just appearing in it
entries.read: What isn't in the Design Museum's new show says as much as what is. Guest curator Charlene Prempeh cut dozens of Black designers she respects from The Nue Black Aesthetic, keeping sixteen whose work shares specific themes rather than a shared identity: more than 100 objects across furniture, architecture, tailoring and sculpture, opening November 6, 2026. Prempeh, author of Now You See Me: An Introduction to 100 Years of Black Design, built the show to argue against the idea of Black design as merely crafty; Bianca Saunders' Met Gala suit for Usher sits inside a section called Rethinking the System, not one called craft. It opens in November. The room hasn't caught up to that argument yet.

entries.name: Daylight Come
entries.benchmark: a CROWN next to Noname Book Club — same diasporic literary register, memory over hagiography
entries.read: Harry Belafonte's been dead three years and just landed on the bestseller list anyway. Daylight Come, Joshua Jelly-Schapiro's biography of the Harlem-born son of Caribbean immigrants who turned calypso into American pop and bankrolled the civil rights movement's road trips, published August 4th at 384 pages. Named a Most Anticipated Book of 2026 by The New York Times before a single copy shipped.

entries.name: Judah Weston
entries.benchmark: a TORCH next to Fetty P Franklin — same underground-rap lane, still building the catalog the buzz is asking for
entries.read: Judah Weston already has an eight-city East Coast run booked for September, Lexington through Raleigh, off a discography that's mostly loosies. Why So Much Hate, his thirteen-song project with producer IsoKeys, dropped July 17th and plays like a Lower East Side kid working out his own myth in public: a felony arrest at twelve, a single mom and three brothers, the hop between boroughs. "Thug" pulled 20K views on a warning-shot video that felt bigger than its number; the comments called him early before the songs had finished cohering into a voice. The tour is real. The catalog isn't a statement yet. Come back after the run and see whether the road turned the loosies into an album.

issues.forecast: A twelve-year hotel renovation and an eleven-minute rap record are teaching the same lesson this week: patience reads as scarcity, and scarcity still beats volume.
come_up: Archival inheritance: Denim Tears rebuilding André Leon Talley's wardrobe instead of just citing him
Compression over runtime: Fatboi Sharif & E L U C I D fitting six songs into eleven minutes and calling it finished
Foundation-building before platform-chasing: 603 Arts opening with migration as premise, not a mission statement
decline: Quarterly hotel openings measured in room count, not room use
A feature ledger mistaken for a body of work
Tribute framing used as a shortcut past actually writing inside a lineage
issues.climate: Patience over volume, again: a mansion closed since 2014 outlasts a hotel-brand news cycle built on quarterly launches, and a duo compresses six songs into one file rather than pad a deluxe edition nobody asked for. The counter-read is a feature ledger — Keen Streetz's résumé already reads like a career and still hasn't produced the one object that would make the case in a single sitting.

entries.name: Denim Tears
entries.benchmark: already on the 50 — this reads directly against its own canon slot, no stretch needed
entries.read: Denim Tears spent August teaching a lookbook to grieve properly. Tremaine Emory's Fall/Winter 2026 collection, previewed August 3 and shipping across five drops beginning August 14, rebuilds André Leon Talley's wardrobe piece by piece — a Billionaire Boys Club sweater Talley wore to New York Fashion Week in 2010, reconstructed alongside a Stüssy collaboration, a panther-print chino, and Denim Tears' own signature parka. The brand's whole method has always been this: clothing as an inheritance document rather than a costume. Talley died in 2022 at 73; the collection doesn't costume his death, it continues his argument — that Black taste-making deserves the same reverence white couture houses give their own dead. Models include Edward Buchanan and André Walker, both of whom actually knew him, which is the difference between a tribute and a séance. Emory has spent three years turning Denim Tears from a Levi's collaboration into a publishing house that happens to sell clothes; this is his most explicit thesis yet on who gets remembered, and who has to be re-remembered on purpose.

entries.name: Fatboi Sharif & E L U C I D
entries.benchmark: a CROWN next to Chris Crack — same instinct, prolific and abstract, more interested in mood than a hook
entries.read: Fatboi Sharif and E L U C I D turned eleven minutes into a statement on August 12, and streaming services list it as one track out of spite. Invasion Body Camera compresses six songs — Rage, the title cut featuring Beans, God Is an Eternal Concorde — into a single unskippable file, East New York production wrapped around Rahway's most consistently unsettling voice. E L U C I D wrote, produced, engineered, and mixed the whole thing himself, which explains why it sounds like one nervous system instead of a placement reel. It's Sharif's fourth release of 2026. Nobody's asking him to slow down; the catalog is the argument.

entries.name: The Cataclysm of Binary Star Systems — 603 Arts Foundation
entries.benchmark: a FLAME next to One54 — different medium, same instinct: build the infrastructure before asking for the platform
entries.read: A new foundation opened its account on August 8 by imagining the end of the sun. The Cataclysm of Binary Star Systems, the inaugural show from 603 Arts Foundation at Nunu Fine Art in SoHo, gathers twelve artists from nine countries across Asia, Latin America, and their diasporas — four showing in the US for the first time — around a premise borrowed from astrophysics: two stars close enough to strip each other of matter until nothing habitable is left. Founders Kate Lee and Clovis Lima Jr. are betting the foundation's first move on migration read as inheritance, not tragedy. On view through August 29.

entries.name: Keen Streetz
entries.benchmark: a TORCH next to Starlito — grinding, catalog-over-hype, no single mythologized project
entries.read: Keen Streetz doesn't chase a lane so much as furnish everyone else's. The Far Rockaway rapper turned up on Rick Hyde's “FAKE LUV” on August 11, one more credit in a features ledger that already runs through Jim Jones, Dave East, and Conway the Machine. No single project carries the weight; the guest list does.

entries.name: Palais Jamaï, Fès
entries.benchmark: the nearest thing on the 50 is Fortnum & Mason, and it isn't close — continuity is the story in both, but Ducasse's name is doing the marketing here, not an unbroken institution
entries.read: Palais Jamaï closed in 2014, and Fès waited twelve years for the state railway company that owns it to finish rebuilding a Grand Vizier's mansion into something guests could sleep in again. The restoration reopens this spring under the Preferred Hotels Legend Collection, with Alain Ducasse running the kitchens: 94 rooms carved from a 19th-century Fes el-Bali compound, zellij tilework and carved cedar intact from the original build. Still, the tilework is the tilework. Come back when the reviews are in.

issues.forecast: What stopped working this week is the release as an event. The objects holding attention are salvage jobs and long installs: a Sudanese cassette library rebuilt in Oakland, a tapestry that has hung in one Cape Town atrium since October, a rap catalog that took eleven records to arrive.
issues.climate: Salvage over supply. The week's strongest work was built to outlast the calendar rather than feed it: a war-era discography digitized one cassette at a time, a commission measured in months on view, cover art still drawn by hand now that the prompt is free. The counter-read is a Memphis album released from federal custody, where the attention sits entirely on the case file and the record is the smaller object in the room.
come_up: Salvage archiving: diaspora kids digitizing analog media faster than the institutions can
The year-long install: commissions measured in months on view, not opening-night traffic
Hand-drawn cover art as a brand position now that generation costs nothing
decline: Generative cover art bolted onto a finished record
The album as a filing in an ongoing case
Archive talk with no digitization budget behind it

entries.name: Sudan Tapes Archive
entries.benchmark: a CROWN next to Black Film Archive — the same recovery instinct, pointed at cassette tape instead of celluloid
entries.read: A $20 cassette-to-USB converter is doing work that Sudan's national institutions can no longer do. Haneen Sidahmed, a Sudanese American archivist in Oakland, started digitizing her father's tapes in lockdown, learning restoration from forum posts written by hobbyists in Wisconsin and Mississippi. That became the Sudan Tapes Archive: her parents' cassettes, tapes she pulled out of Souq Omdurman months before the market burned, and donations from other diaspora families. Since war reached Khartoum in 2023 the museums have been looted and the libraries burned, and archaeologists warned this month that the pyramids at Meroë are deteriorating from neglect. Sidahmed calls it a war on collective memory and treats every restored track as a small reversal. The scholarship is real rather than sentimental. She can tell you that Mahmoud Abdelaziz's Sakat Al-Rabab (1995) was recorded by a Russian orchestra that learned Sudanese repertoire, and that a generation of Sudanese violinists trained under North Korean instructors posted to Khartoum. Her listening parties run outdoors with guiding questions at each station, because the tradition was communal: one family, one tape deck, one tape. The gap is that nobody with a budget is doing this.

entries.name: Rome Streetz — Sock It 2 My Pocket
entries.benchmark: a FLAME next to Starlito — same lane, a career built on catalog depth rather than one mythologized project
entries.read: Eleven records deep, Rome Streetz finally sounds like a man who owns the building. Sock It 2 My Pocket landed on July 17 through Nas's Mass Appeal: fifteen tracks, forty-three minutes, no deluxe edition, with Pete Rock, Havoc, Conductor Williams and 9th Wonder on the loops and Styles P, Lloyd Banks and Westside Gunn passing through. Pitchfork gave it 73; the user score sits at 79 across 1,396 ratings, which is the more useful number for a rapper whose audience buys physical copies rather than streams. London-born, Brooklyn-raised, he still writes like every bar is a debt being collected. The consensus that this is his best since Kiss the Ring is, this time, correct.

entries.name: The Procession — Rita Mawuena Benissan
entries.benchmark: a FLAME next to Lauren Halsey — monumental scale built out of community iconography, made with the people whose iconography it is
entries.read: Suspended inside a converted 1921 grain silo, nine storeys of sliced concrete, is a tapestry you can see straight through. The Procession went up in the atrium at Zeitz MOCAA in Cape Town on October 25 and comes down October 25, a full year on view: 400kg of sheer fabric and embroidered canvas, patterned with seagulls and palm fronds, drawn from the canopy of royal umbrellas that shade Akan chiefs in public procession. Rita Mawuena Benissan, born in Abidjan in 1995 and trained in apparel and textile design, founded Si Hene in 2020 to preserve Ghanaian chieftaincy culture and worked on the reopening of the National Museum of Ghana in 2022. Thirteen artisans are named as contributors. The crediting is the practice, not a footnote to it.

entries.name: Niyi Okeowo
entries.benchmark: a FLAME next to Mason Prince — same design-studio register, a house style built on typography and restraint
entries.read: Niyi Okeowo starts with the lyrics and ends with a typeface. The Lagos designer behind Fireboy DML's Apollo, Wande Coal's Realms and two volumes of Show Dem Camp's Palmwine Music calls a cover a dialogue between artist and designer, which is a polite way of saying a prompt cannot have one. He also co-founded the magazine Get Unruly and runs creative at Kuda, a Nigerian payments company. The hedge is the read: cover work alone no longer pays.

entries.name: Pooh Shiesty — All Eyes on Shiest
entries.benchmark: the nearest thing on the 50 is Fetty P Franklin, and it isn't close — same street register, opposite relationship to scale and to a major label
entries.read: Pooh Shiesty can still write a hook that works as threat and prayer at once, and “Last Man Breathin” is the proof: piano, violin, a man counting his own release date against a friend's 75-year sentence. All Eyes on Shiest arrived on August 7 through 1017 Global and Atlantic, sixteen tracks assembled and released while he sits in federal custody in Dallas awaiting a February 22, 2027 trial on kidnapping and robbery charges involving the founder of the label that signed him. Almost all of the attention is on the case file. The record is the smaller object in the room, and it plays like a placeholder cut to fit a news cycle rather than a first album. Come back after the trial date and see whether there is a body of work behind the headline.

issues.forecast: The strongest work this week is not a debut but a set of severances: a rapper breaking up with his therapist, his barber and his doctor in the same verse; a novelist giving a twenty-year friendship the weight normally reserved for a marriage.
issues.climate: Leaving over arriving. The week's two best-written objects are both breakups, and neither is about a lover, which is what makes them useful: each is specific about which relationship is ending and what it cost. Underneath sits a quieter question of custody. Who keeps the material once the scene, the friendship or the label is gone. An Accra archivist answers by repairing the damaged prints by hand; a Madeiran collective answers by building the infrastructure its island never had. The counter-read is a $45 record with no listening history behind it, sold on the ritual of ownership before a single disc has shipped.
come_up: The platonic breakup as a serious literary subject, given the weight usually held back for romance
Repair as archive method: the damage left visible instead of retouched out
Peripheral labels underwriting their own scenes when the festival circuit will not
decline: The keepsake pressed before anyone has played the song twice
Eco-material claims standing in for a spec sheet
African hip hop framed as an arrival story rather than a thirty-year record

entries.name: Open Mike Eagle & Kenny Segal — DOOMED!
entries.benchmark: Chris Crack in the underground-rap lane; the same Chicago absurdism, held to one long argument instead of a dozen short ones
entries.read: Fifteen tracks in, Open Mike Eagle has broken up with his therapist, his barber and his primary care physician. Only one of those was a romance. DOOMED! landed August 14 on Backwoodz Studioz, the first full-length from two men who have been friends in Los Angeles for almost twenty years and found each other in the orbit of Project Blowed. Segal produces all of it and refuses the beat switch: dusty loops, muted jazz, worn samples kept at a simmer so the comic-book framing has somewhere to land. Seven reviews in, the critical average sits at 81, which is the room agreeing with something it can plainly hear. The track to sit with is "Unfinished Concrete Initials," where the stick breaks before the names are finished and the concrete sets anyway.

entries.name: Selorm Attikpo — Mending to Preserve
entries.benchmark: Black Film Archive — one person's catalog hardening into the institution nobody funded
entries.read: The verb in the title is literal. Selorm Attikpo repairs the photographs before he hangs them: damaged prints from three decades of Ghanaian hip hop, physically mended, then shown beside the recordings and the paper that survived with them. Mending to Preserve opens Friday August 21, 6 to 8pm, at the African Diaspora Art Museum of Atlanta on University Avenue in Pittsburgh Yards. Attikpo, who works as Selormjay, founded yoyo tinz in Accra in 2013 and has built a personal archive of roughly 10,000 files on the scene since. He put on Ghana's first hip hop festival in 2018. He has been researching a permanent hip hop museum for Ghana as a Villa Albertine resident, which is what put him in Atlanta: two cities written out of the hip hop story for years, both of which wrote themselves back in. What separates this from the usual archive show is that the damage stays visible. A mended print does not pretend the neglect never happened. It says somebody came back for it. Free, Thursday to Saturday, noon to five.

entries.name: Téa Mutonji — My Person
entries.benchmark: Noname Book Club — the diasporic reading lane on the 50; this is the novel it would set
entries.read: Tania asks Margot to unknow her. They have been best friends for over twenty years, Margot's family owns the apartment Tania lives in, and the request arrives while the two of them are laying the table for their monthly dinner. My Person is Téa Mutonji's first novel, 288 pages, out August 11 from Putnam, seven years after the story collection Shut Up You're Pretty. Mutonji was born in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and raised in Scarborough, and she is exact about the Canadian shape of the problem: prejudice that arrives as extravagant generosity and quietly erodes whoever accepts it. The novel gives a friendship the psychological weight usually held for a marriage, then lets neither woman off.

entries.name: Colectivo Casa Amarela
entries.benchmark: CD Masterizzato — the physical music object as the whole argument, here at 30-copy scale
entries.read: Madeira sits closer to Morocco than to Lisbon, and for two decades the island's experimental calendar ran on a single festival programmed mostly for visitors. Colectivo Casa Amarela started in 2015 because the island's own musicians could not get on it. Past forty releases now, mostly cassettes, some in plaster shells sculpted by Mafalda Melim, who runs the label from Lisbon with Bruno Aires. Vomir's first pressing sold out in an hour.

entries.name: Suno Vinyl
entries.benchmark: Moises AI is the nearest thing on the 50, and the distance is the read: Moises sells work to makers, this sells an object to owners
entries.read: Suno has read the room correctly. People want to hold the thing, and a file will not do it, so on August 6 the company opened a waitlist: up to 46 minutes from your library, pressed to a 12-inch black PETG disc, sleeve and labels of your own design, around $45 plus shipping. The pitch reads "Some songs deserve more than a stream." Missing is everything a record buyer asks next. No plant named, no mastering chain, no weight, no tolerances, and nothing shipped yet. A Munich court ruled against the company in GEMA's case this month. The object is doing the argument the catalog has not won. Come back when the first discs land and somebody plays one twice.

issues.forecast: Peckham on Sunday, Ladbroke Grove in three weeks, a Rolex microsite that went live on Tuesday: the first two are the end of something long, the third is the start of a month of drops.
issues.climate: Duration over drop. The work holding up this week was built on a clock nobody else was watching: a mural painted straight onto a gallery wall in May and painted over on Sunday, forty years behind a Portobello salon compressed into a six-day retrospective, fifteen songs put out on ten days' notice with no interview attached. Against that sits the release calendar as a medium in itself, twelve one-of-one watches metered across August so the announcement can happen twelve times, and a marketplace whose house label is thirty percent off while its tenants hold price. The counter-read is not that the fast work is bad. It is that attention has concentrated on the placements while the bodies of work behind them stayed the same size.
come_up: The unannounced record: fifteen tracks out on ten days' notice with no interview cycle behind them
The retrospective assembled by the community it is about, with clients sitting in the curator's chair
Free shows with a hard closing date, doing what a fair week cannot
decline: The one-of-one release schedule, where the drop calendar is the artwork
Marketplaces whose house label undercuts the tenants it was built to pay
Placement volume read as a body of work

entries.name: Cleo Sol — Gentlewoman
entries.benchmark: a CROWN next to Baby Rose — the same diasporic soul register on the 50, held at a lower volume and a longer breath
entries.read: There is no press cycle attached to this one. Gentlewoman went up today on Forever Living Originals, ten days after a phone clip announced it: fifteen tracks, Inflo producing, Chronixx and Dave Okumu among the credited writers, no interviews. The absence is the method, not shyness. Heaven and Gold both landed on days' notice in 2023; this one got ten, which still counts as a long runway by her standards, and it lets the record behave like a record instead of a campaign. It is her first solo album since Gold; Sault's Chapter 1 came in January out of the same house, same producer. The songs run on repetition and reassurance rather than hooks, so they improve on the fourth pass and disappear inside a playlist — the album is the unit and she has never pretended otherwise. Fifteen tracks is a lot of calm to ask for in a row, and the honest risk is that calm reads as sameness somewhere around track eleven. The room is loud here and the room is right. The test lands in November: still in rotation, or filed under respected.

entries.name: Paulo Nimer Pjota — Encantados
entries.benchmark: a CROWN next to Lauren Halsey — monumental work built out of vernacular signage and street iconography, São Paulo instead of South Central
entries.read: The mural comes down on Sunday. Pjota painted it directly onto the walls of the South London Gallery's Main Gallery, and when Encantados closes on August 23 it gets covered over: five months up, free, no booking, gone. He describes the method as sampling and means it literally. He was a graffiti writer in São José do Rio Preto before he was a painter, and he builds canvases the way a producer builds a beat — loop a piece of art history, drop something new over it. A speaker stack with reggae written across it. A three-headed animal working a trumpet, a horn and a drum at once. The gallery screened Wild Style in July alongside the show, which is how you know they read it right. Peckham, until Sunday.

entries.name: Charlotte Mensah — Community Matters
entries.benchmark: a FLAME next to Material Culture — heritage craft with a documented lineage, except the object here is a room on Portobello Road
entries.read: Splinters, days before her sixteenth birthday. Charlotte Mensah started at the first Black salon in Britain in 1986, trained under Winston Isaacs at the London College of Fashion, and has run Hair Lounge on Portobello Road for twenty-five years. Community Matters opens at Ladbroke Hall on September 8 and closes on the 13th. The detail that decides it: the curator, Madeleine Haddon of V&A East, is a client, and so is the exhibition designer. A retrospective assembled by the people who sat in the chair is a different object from one assembled about them. Forty years, three Afro Hairdresser of the Year titles, first Black woman in the British Hairdressing Hall of Fame. The show is six days long.

entries.name: Lowheads
entries.benchmark: the nearest thing on the 50 is Gr8, and the distance is the read: Gr8 earns authority by cutting the floor down, this earns reach by opening it up
entries.read: Los Angeles, two hundred-odd labels, one checkout, and the money goes to the designer. That is the real product: an $85 cut-off from a label nobody has heard of gets ordered, and the person who sewed it gets paid, which is harder to build than a feed. Founded 2020, an apply-to-sell page open to anyone, an iPhone app, a podcast. Then read the footer. The store's own TikTok handle is @cuts_garments — Cuts is the house label — and this week Cuts sits at thirty percent off across the board while the tenant brands hold full price. A landlord who opens a shop in his own building is not only a landlord. The audience showed up for an edit and the edit is now competing with itself. The number to watch is the front page: two hundred brands is a floor, forty is a position.

entries.name: Slawn — The Rolex Multiverse
entries.benchmark: the nearest thing on the 50 is Corteiz, and it is a drop-logic match rather than a studio one — Clint419 is literally one of the twelve
entries.read: Nobody moves an image faster. Slawn's caricatures have been on a BRIT statuette, the FA Cup, Nigeria's World Cup kit and, since Tuesday, a Playboi Carti chain; the Rolex Multiverse puts them on twelve one-of-one watches released one at a time across August. His 2024 Rolex run sold out in four minutes. The placements have traveled further than the paintings. Come back when there is a show with no logo in the room.

issues.forecast: The best object on the board this week was stolen: six dilly bags woven from British Museum floor plans, lifted two pounds at a time by a network of friends. Custody over access — the work that held up was made by people taking their material back rather than asking to see it.
come_up: The woven archive: paper turned to string, museum floor plans turned to objects
Self-written lineage: writers documenting their own pioneers on their own wall
Buffalo's second bench: hook men stepping out as lead artists
decline: Graffiti as ticketed spectacle: €20 entry, gift shop at the exit
The guest-list album: features stacked where a thesis should be
Prize coverage that names the top winner and skips the six category winners
issues.climate: Custody over access. Four of the five entries turn on who is allowed to hold the material: a Larrakia weaver turning stolen museum maps into dilly bags, eleven Philadelphia writers painting their own lineage onto a wall on Willow Street instead of waiting for an institution to do it, a Palestinian archivist working from footage nobody else kept. Against that sits Paris, where fifty years of graffiti is ticketed at €20 with a shop at the exit. The counter-read is not that the Paris show is wrong; it is thorough, and thorough is rare. Collecting a movement and continuing one are simply different jobs, and only one of them is happening on a wall this month.

entries.name: Jenna Mayilema Lee — Taking back taken
entries.benchmark: heritage-craft lane — Material Culture, and this sits at the sharper end of it
entries.read: Jenna Mayilema Lee spent five years learning to turn paper into string, and the paper she chose was the British Museum's own floor plan. That map carries a suggested donation of two pounds; Lee took one without paying, then had family and friends flying to London take more on her behalf until she had enough to weave six dilly bags. Taking back taken won the $15,000 Work on Paper Award at the Telstra NATSIAAs in Darwin on August 7, one of seven prizes drawn from 64 finalists and 221 entries. Lee is Larrakia, Karrajarri and Wardaman, working in Melbourne and off Country, which is the practical reason the material is paper and not pandanus: following her ancestors means being expert in the resources around you, and hers is a house full of books. The detail that decides it: she describes the collecting network she assembled as not unlike the way empire sent people out to gather world culture. The bags take the form of the objects she used to book appointments to see in museum storerooms. On show at MAGNT until January 24.

entries.name: Mohanad Yaqubi — Revolutionaries Never Die
entries.benchmark: Black Film Archive
entries.read: Jocelyne Saab emailed Mohanad Yaqubi in October 2018 asking him to make something with her. She died two months later, before he answered. Revolutionaries Never Die is the reply, assembled out of what she left: 11 boxes holding 115 film and audio reels lodged with the CNC in Paris, shot across Lebanon, Palestine, Iran and Western Sahara. Yaqubi credits it as a letter rather than a film, and the credit is the tell. It ran 80 minutes at its Locarno world premiere and took the Filmmakers of the Present special jury prize on August 15, from an edition running 233 films chosen out of a record 7,759 submissions. An archivist who spends years getting someone else's footage into a conversation is doing a different job from directing. Locarno just paid for it as authorship.

entries.name: Construction of Style — Mural Arts Philadelphia
entries.benchmark: Lauren Halsey
entries.read: Eleven writers painted a wall at 412 North 2nd Street in Philadelphia and used it to tell their own history. Construction of Style, put together by Phil Asbury for Mural Arts, carries work designed by Dawud Anyabwile of BrothaMan Comics, Sew SM, Distort BAMC, Busta, Rew, Imse, Saoka, Diana Gonzalez, Efrain Herrera and Kien Nguyen, with a final panel honoring Cornbread, Cool Earl, Tity, Sub, Cone ICP and Lewis. Amina Tawasil, the Columbia anthropologist whose fieldwork follows writers across Philadelphia, New York and urban New Jersey, recorded the audio tour. A discipline that has spent sixty years being explained by outsiders here supplies the wall and the commentary both. Free, outdoors, still going up, parking on Willow.

entries.name: GooseByTheWay — Nature Boy
entries.benchmark: Starlito
entries.read: A hook man steps out front. Nature Boy, out July 17, runs ten tracks with Conway the Machine anchoring three of them including the opener "203", and Fuego Base taking the sharpest verse on "Walk Ups". Goose writes money as obligation rather than trophy: back years, fed kids, debts with names attached. Buffalo has a deep bench; this is the season it starts releasing under its own name.

entries.name: BEYOND THE STREETS Paris
entries.benchmark: places lane — The Shed, and the distance is that one commissions while this one collects
entries.read: The archival job is done properly here: 3,600 square meters of the Grande Halle de la Villette, more than 100 artists, and ephemera that has spent decades in boxes, running from Futura 2000 and Barry McGee to Vhils and Felipe Pantone. Entry starts at €20 and the exit is a shop assembled with Sarah Andelman. The Paris run closes this month. Attention has concentrated on the survey rather than the practice: fifty years of a discipline gets a ticketed hall, while the writers still working get a wall and a tag on someone's feed. Come back when that same square footage goes to a living crew with a commissioning budget.

issues.forecast: Two Moroccos this month: in a village an hour up the Ourika valley an architect is rebuilding a school in stone, with the pupils' parents laying the walls, and in a Sandton exhibition hall a Marrakech studio was crowned Africa's designer of the year. Both are Moroccan craft. Only one of them names the masons.
come_up: The named crew: masons, cutters and plasterers credited on the object they made
Solo billing after a decade of split covers: the writing asked to carry the record alone
Invented place names doing what real ones cannot: fiction as a way to hold a loss
decline: “In collaboration with local artisans” as a credit line
Craft priced in a convention hall a continent from the workshop
Reconstruction reported only as units completed
issues.climate: Naming over branding. Three of the five entries turn on whose name ends up on the object: an architect who puts the pupils' parents on the wall crew at Setti Fatma, a rapper who spent ten years splitting album covers with one producer at a time and finally kept one for himself, a novelist who gives every member of a scattered family their own chapter instead of a narrator. Against that sits a Marrakech studio collecting the continent's design prize of the year with its makers described in the plural and left unnamed. The counter-read is not that the work is thin; the ceramics are good and the workshops are real. It is that the attention arrived at the signature before it arrived at the hands. The fifth entry sits on the same question from the other side: a studio built so that a track has more than one author in it from the first bar.

entries.name: Salima Naji — the school at Setti Fatma
entries.benchmark: heritage-craft lane — Material Culture is the nearest thing on the 50, and the 50 has no architect on it at all
entries.read: The masons rebuilding the school at Setti Fatma are the parents of the children who will sit in it. That is Salima Naji's method rather than a detail of it. She is an architect and anthropologist who has spent twenty years restoring the collective granaries of southern Morocco, and who rebuilt the kasbah at Agadir Oufella on a wood-and-stone system rather than the concrete that crushed people there in 1960. Setti Fatma sits an hour up the Ourika valley from Marrakech and was wrecked by the quake of September 8, 2023, three years old in a fortnight. The state's answer across Al Haouz has been volume: official counts put the province past 90 percent of some 24,000 homes rebuilt or repaired, mostly in block and cement. Naji's answer is stone, earth, palm fiber and a crew trained on the job, so the technique stays in the village after she leaves. ARVHA gave her its international prize in January, which is the room arriving late rather than early. Check in September whether the school has pupils in it.

entries.name: Ransom — The Price of Clarity
entries.benchmark: underground-rap lane — Starlito, the same career shape: two decades in, no radio record, the catalog is the argument
entries.read: Seventeen tracks, fifty-nine minutes, and no producer's name on the cover. That last part is the news. Randy Nicholls has spent most of a decade making albums the other way round — one rapper, one producer, a whole record — with Nicholas Craven, DJ Premier, Conductor Williams, Harry Fraud, V Don and Big Ghost Ltd, four of them in 2025 alone. The Price of Clarity, out August 19 through Momentum Entertainment, is billed as his first official solo album; the last full-length with nobody's name beside his was 2022. The trade-off is audible. A one-producer record has a single weather system, and this one has five or six hands on it and asks the writing to hold the thing together instead. It mostly does. He is forty-five and writes like it, which in a lane built on teenage stamina is the scarcer skill: the subject here is what honesty costs after you have already told the truth about the obvious things. Nobody is playing this on the radio. Nobody was ever going to. Come back in six months and see whether the solo billing sticks or he goes back to splitting the credit.

entries.name: Dreams of Ayn Ara — Sara Abou Ghazal
entries.benchmark: global-diaspora lane — Noname Book Club, the same instinct for the small press over the front table
entries.read: Every chapter belongs to a different member of the Abu Sukkar family, and the family is scattered: Zein al-Abidin in Stockholm, his son Nidal in Paris, the matriarch Zahra holding what is left, Salwa in Beirut digging backwards through Facebook toward Ayn Ara, the Galilee village they came from. The village is invented. That choice does work a real place name could not, because the subject is not one loss but the shape of it, repeated down four generations from a camp in Shatila. Katharine Halls translates, and her record is the reason to trust the English: Rotten Evidence, The Dove's Necklace, a Banipal prize. The specialist room got here first and got it right, which is the job a small press is for. Feminist Press, August 18, 2026, hardcover, $17.95.

entries.name: Riffle
entries.benchmark: creator-ai-tools lane — Koala Sampler, the same instinct: an MPC in a place nobody expected one
entries.read: The pitch is a grudge. Riffle's founders say a DAW hands you a cockpit when all you wanted was an instrument. Their answer went public on August 12 after three months of early access with 7,000 musicians: browser only, no download, real-time multiplayer on an infinite canvas, and an MPC-style sampler that saves custom kits across boards. The assistant reads your MIDI, which is where it either earns the room or joins it.

entries.name: LRNCE
entries.benchmark: heritage-craft lane — Tamera; LRNCE is the bigger operation and the more finished object
entries.read: LRNCE makes good things. Hand-painted ceramics, zellige, plaster, iron and wood, produced with workshops in and around Marrakech since 2013, the irregularities left in rather than sanded out. Decorex Africa named it Designer of the Year for 2026 and gave it both editions, Cape Town in June and Sandton from July 30 to August 2. The gap is that the credit stops at two names. Laurence Leenaert and Ayoub Boualam are the studio; the potters, the zellige cutters and the plasterers are “Moroccan artisans,” plural and unnamed, in every notice of the award. Come back when a collection ships with the workshops named on it.

issues.forecast: Two numbers set the board this week: CHF 148,500 for a platinum wristwatch that does not exist yet, and roughly £85,000 a year for a sound system that plays for free on a Notting Hill corner. Both figures are the true cost of an object. Only one of them is a price.
come_up: Published capacity: four watches a year, stated in the release rather than buried in it
Free entry as an editorial position, not a subsidy — the laureate charging nothing at home
The two-minute rap song as discipline: twenty-one tracks, forty-nine minutes, no filler
